messages.subject: projections (datums) & areas,
parts:
Hi,

informative topics and discussion; thanks.

For projections, perhaps try:
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Map_projection

Re. Shapefiles in Distance Sampling software, I would suggest the following
logic perhaps:

DISTANCE SAMPLING software should only use what it is given, e.g. from the
GIS and outside. Hefty manipulations of these files should all be left to
elsewhere, e.g. GIS (Unless one knows what one is doing, I would not suggest
start modifying code or settings). In Distance Sampling, I just
import/export Shapefiles as a whole.

For a reader on Shapefiles and GRIDS, see for instance
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shapefile
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESRI_grid

So I 'trust' the GIS system on the projection issue. This is because a)
that's what the business of the software company is for decades, b) they
have developed much better tools there, and c) GIS is highly tested by now,
specifically on the projection issue.

It's indeed a (convenient) flaw somehow to assume Density would be a metrics
that happens in a plain 2 dimensional setting (it never is in nature...not
even in the ocean: These are either rugged or at least curved), or that the
area would be consistent without holes (e.g. lakes or glaciers).

Re. projections, I think confusion can come in when Lat Lon's gets
interpreted as Coordinates in Meters, or vice versa. Some projections still
deal with feet even. But this is rel. easy to recognize because Lat Lon's
are only in the 180 max (or 360 max) range. Watch for the decimal notation
in the degrees, as well as in the minutes (two different things: You can
easily check whether the minutes go above 60...adjust your GPS to decimal
degrees).

To some, and as relevant as above, the notion of the underlying Geographic
Datum (e.g. WGS 1984, that's what GOOGLE uses; or earlier ones such as NAD
1927 and NAD1983) might matter much.

It's a common experience that these Geographic Datums either get ignored or
pooled, e.g. when matching maps and in GPS work (combining decimal lat lons
but different geographic datums).
This will result in fuzziness of the data, e.g. +100 m (depends where one is
on Earth), and I assume it could affect the area estimates.

I assume that these things should matter for us because they affect i) the
assigned distance/area for density estimates, as well as ii) the area
extrapolated to for overall population estimates; right?
I am curious about the confidence intervals.

I really wish to learn more about these things. Perhaps you have some
thoughts or know some publications on the issue ?

Overall, I believe that (FGDC NBII) Metadata are crucial for these things
(GIS files, projections, DS project and density estimates) and for a
reliable, transparent and trustworthy science and management.

Very best
F.

-----Original Message-----
From: Wildlife abundance estimation using distance sampling techniques.
[mailto:DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK] On Behalf Of Eric Rexstad
Sent: Thursday, May 08, 2008 5:36 AM
To: DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK
Subject: Re: [DIST-SAMP] Survey design and map projections

Winston:

Hello again Winston; sounds like you're hard at work designing a survey
for your 'roos. I'm weak on my GIS knowledge, but I'll give a whirl
with your questions.

Kay, Winston wrote:
> > I have been using DISTANCE's survey design features and have a couple of
> > questions about projections.
> >
> > 1. Under File|Project properties|Geographic tab there is a "Parameter"
> > button under the "Maps and Geographic calculations" section of the
> > dialogue box where you can specify values for the false easting, false
> > northing, central meridian and standard parallel 1. Is the "Standard
> > Parallel 1" parameter the same as the "Scale" or "Latitude of Origin"
> > parameter used by ArcGIS/ArcMap?
> >
No, it is not the case that standard parallel 1 is the same as scale or
latitude of origin. Creep inside any "*.prj" file (can be opened with
Notepad), you will see each of the bits in the Geographic tab expressed
therein.
> > 2. I have imported a shapefile in a geographic coordinate system
> > (decimal degrees) into DISTANCE and projected it for the purpose of
> > distance calculations. For the same shapefile, ArcMap calculates the
> > polygon area as 628 sq. km using a Mercator projection but distance
> > calculates the "Stratum Area" as 773 sq. km. I am assuming the stratum
> > area is the same as the polygon area in which case why is there such a
> > big difference in the calculated area?
> >
Someone more knowledgeable on this subject will undoubtedly weigh in
here, but I think what you've described is area calculation taking place
in two different projections (ArcMap used a Mercator projection to
obtain the 773 figure), while Distance is using *unprojected* degrees to
compute the 628 figure. That is the reason for projection, to make the
calculations you are describing comparable.
> > 3. If I have projected a geographic coordinate shapefile with DISTANCE
> > for the purpose calculating distances, do the x-y coordinates generated
> > by line sampler automatically generate these values as unprojected
> > geographic coordinates?
> >
The coordinates produced by the survey design engine will be in the same
projection as that of the shapefile used to describe the study area.
Take a look at Chapter 3 of the "Distance users guide" you will see an
example of designing a survey using the survey design engine, and you
will be greeted with the information "Note that the new samplers have
been added to the project as a new data layer, and this new data layer
has an associated GIS shapefile, so this may be a more convenient format
for exporting to other systems such as GPS. "
> > Thanks for your help.
> >
> > Winston
